name: Eggs
summary: Protein, with choline and lutein in the yolk; in trials, eggs raised the eye's protective pigment slightly. Eating more raises LDL cholesterol a little, but up to about an egg a day wasn't clearly linked with heart disease in large studies.
inIt: An egg is protein in the white and the yolk, plus fat in the yolk. The food table this app uses lists the white (boiled) with no fat at all and the yolk (boiled) with 32.6 g of fat per 100 g.
Eggs are a major source of dietary cholesterol. A review funded by the British Egg Industry Council gives 177 mg of cholesterol in a medium egg; the food table this app uses doesn't list cholesterol.
The yolk is rich in choline, mostly as phosphatidylcholine (lecithin): 285 mg per 100 g of egg in the same industry-funded review. Choline isn't in the food table this app uses.

The yolk holds lutein and zeaxanthin, yellow pigments (carotenoids) that collect in the centre of the retina. How much depends on what the hens are fed: in a French trial, standard eggs had 0.12 mg of lutein each and eggs from hens fed lutein 0.96 mg. Lutein and zeaxanthin aren't in the food table this app uses.

The food table does list protein, vitamin D, vitamin B12, selenium, iodine, retinol (vitamin A), folate, riboflavin and a small amount of the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA. In it, the vitamin D, the retinol and most of the vitamin B12, iron, zinc, iodine and selenium are in the yolk; the boiled white has no vitamin D or retinol.
Like every food, eggs hold compounds no food table tracks. Studies of people eating eggs include all of them; studies of single nutrients from eggs (choline or lutein capsules) don't.

history.use: Raw egg or egg white spread on burns
history.note: No trial we found has tested raw egg on burns, and nothing on this page covers it. The survey's authors note that the first aid backed by the literature is cool running water for 20 minutes within 3 hours of the burn, and call for research into the safety of traditional remedies.

history.use: A dressing of egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine on gunshot wounds, in place of boiling oil
history.note: Paré ran out of boiling oil, and the next morning the soldiers given his mixture had less pain and swelling than those treated with the oil. That chance comparison mostly showed that boiling oil did harm; no trial has tested whether the egg yolk itself helped, and the findings on this page are about eating eggs.

history.who: United States, 1968 to 2015 (American Heart Association, later the Dietary Guidelines for Americans)
history.use: Advice to eat less than 300 mg of dietary cholesterol a day and no more than three whole eggs a week, to protect the heart
history.note: The egg limit was dropped in 2002 and the cholesterol limit around 2015 (one history cited here is by a former director of the US egg industry's Egg Nutrition Center). Today's evidence is split: in trials eggs raise LDL cholesterol a little (about 5 to 8 mg/dL), but in large cohort studies up to about an egg a day wasn't clearly linked with heart disease or stroke, with some US studies finding a small higher risk.

processing: Yolk or white: the food table lists the boiled white with protein (13 g per 100 g) but no fat, vitamin D or retinol; the yolk holds the fat and most of the vitamins. Studies of egg whites or yolk-free egg substitutes test something different from whole eggs.
Cooking makes egg protein easier to digest. In 10 healthy volunteers, 35.10% of the protein in a raw egg meal escaped digestion in the small intestine, compared with 5.73% of the same meal cooked.

Cooking method changes the measured numbers a little: in the food table, 100 g of egg has 3.2 µg of vitamin D boiled and 1.9 µg fried in sunflower oil, and frying adds fat from the oil (15.7 g of fat per 100 g fried, 9.6 g boiled).

What the hens eat changes the egg. In the ALGOVUE trial, eggs from hens fed lutein and microalgae had 0.96 mg of lutein and 134.4 mg of DHA (an omega-3 fat) each, against 0.12 mg and 37.6 mg in standard eggs. In an 8-week winter trial in 55 adults, eggs from hens fed extra vitamin D kept blood vitamin D from falling, while it fell in the group eating 2 or fewer eggs a week.

Raw and lightly cooked eggs can carry Salmonella bacteria. In the UK, eggs with the British Lion mark come from flocks vaccinated against Salmonella under a code of practice, and UK advice counts them as very low risk even raw; other eggs are advised to be cooked until the white and yolk are solid (see 'Who should be careful').

Choline supplements and lutein capsules are different interventions: the findings on this page come from people eating eggs, and one trial found that a choline supplement raised TMAO while eggs with similar choline didn't.
whatStudiesDid: Cohort studies asked people how often they ate eggs, in food questionnaires, and followed them for years: in three large US cohorts (Nurses' Health Studies and Health Professionals Follow-up Study) for up to 32 years with the questionnaire repeated every few years, comparing at least one egg a day with less than one a month; in the Lifetime Risk Pooling Project (six US cohorts, diet asked about and harmonised across studies) per extra half egg a day; in PURE (21 countries) 7 or more eggs a week against fewer than 1; in the China Kadoorie Biobank daily eaters (usually about 0.76 egg a day) against people who never or rarely ate eggs. Meta-analyses pooled these per extra egg a day. Trials gave people extra eggs on top of their usual diet or in a set diet: 640 mg a day of extra dietary cholesterol from eggs for 30 days (against a placebo with no cholesterol), 2 eggs a day 6 days a week against fewer than 2 eggs a week for 3 to 12 months in people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes (DIABEGG), 6 eggs a week for 12 weeks, 2 and then 4 egg yolks a day for 5 weeks each, 1 egg a day for 90 days or 2 eggs a day for 4 months in the eye trials, and single breakfasts of 0 to 6 egg yolks or 4 hard-boiled eggs a day for 4 weeks in the TMAO trials.

findings.population: Adults without heart disease in long-term cohort studies in the US, Europe and Asia (meta-analyses of up to 3.6 million people)
whyThisGrade: Observational: people chose how many eggs they ate, and egg eaters differ in other ways. In the US cohorts, people who ate more eggs had a higher BMI, used statins less, and ate more red meat, bacon, other processed meat, refined grains and sugar-sweetened drinks

Large studies disagree: the 2020 meta-analysis found no link per egg a day (0.98), the 2022 meta-analysis a small higher risk (1.04, at the edge of significance), and the Lifetime Risk Pooling Project a higher risk per half egg a day

Results vary between studies (heterogeneity 62% to 80%) and by region: no link in US or European cohorts in one meta-analysis, a higher risk in US cohorts in the other, and lower risk in Asian cohorts
Eggs were counted in food questionnaires, often with the foods eaten alongside them; how well studies separated eggs from those foods differs
findings.summary: In three large US cohorts (215,618 people followed for up to 32 years), eating at least one egg a day wasn't linked with heart disease and stroke after accounting for updated lifestyle and the foods eaten with eggs (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.82 to 1.05, against less than one egg a month). In the same paper's meta-analysis (1,720,108 people), each extra egg a day wasn't linked with cardiovascular disease (relative risk 0.98, 0.93 to 1.03): 1.01 (0.96 to 1.06) in US cohorts, 1.05 (0.92 to 1.19) in European ones and 0.92 (0.85 to 0.99) in Asian ones. In contrast, the Lifetime Risk Pooling Project (29,615 US adults, median 17.5 years) found each extra half egg a day went with higher risk of cardiovascular disease (1.06, 1.03 to 1.10), and each extra 300 mg of dietary cholesterol a day too (1.17, 1.09 to 1.26); the egg link disappeared after adjusting for dietary cholesterol (0.99, 0.93 to 1.05), pointing to the cholesterol in eggs. The 2020 authors suggest that study lacked simultaneous control for foods such as red meat and for BMI. A 2022 meta-analysis (3,601,401 people) found 1.04 (1.00 to 1.08) per extra 50-g egg a day, 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) in US cohorts and no link in Asian ones. In 461,213 Chinese adults, daily egg eaters had lower risk than non-eaters (0.89, 0.87 to 0.92), and PURE (146,011 people in 21 countries) found no link for 7 or more eggs a week (major cardiovascular disease 0.92, 0.83 to 1.01).
findings.bottomLine: Across large cohort studies, eating up to about an egg a day wasn't clearly linked with heart disease or stroke overall. Some US studies found a small higher risk, tied to the cholesterol in eggs; Asian studies found lower risk. These are links, not proof.

findings.population: Adults in long-term cohort studies (meta-analysis of 33 cohorts, 2.2 million people), and international cohorts in 50 countries
whyThisGrade: The 2022 meta-analysis authors rated the certainty of their evidence low to moderate
Observational, with self-reported egg intake; people who eat more eggs may differ in diet and habits
Studies disagree: no link overall in two large analyses, but a small higher risk per egg in US-led analyses that also found it for dietary cholesterol
findings.summary: A 2022 meta-analysis of 33 cohort studies (2,216,720 people, 232,408 deaths) found no link between the highest and lowest egg intakes and death from any cause (relative risk 1.02, 95% confidence interval 0.94 to 1.11), heart and blood vessel disease (1.04, 0.87 to 1.23) or stroke (0.81, 0.64 to 1.02), but a higher risk of cancer death (1.20, 1.04 to 1.39); per extra egg a week, risk of death from any cause was 2% higher and of cancer death 4% higher, and of stroke death 4% lower. The authors rated the certainty low to moderate. In PURE (146,011 people in 21 countries), eating 7 or more eggs a week wasn't linked with death (hazard ratio 1.04, 0.94 to 1.15, against fewer than 1 a week), nor in 31,544 people with vascular disease in two international trials (0.88, 0.62 to 1.24). In contrast, the US Lifetime Risk Pooling Project (29,615 adults) found each extra half egg a day went with higher risk of death (1.08, 1.04 to 1.11), and in 27,078 men in the ATBC study each extra 50-g egg a day went with a hazard ratio of 1.06 for death from any cause.
findings.bottomLine: In most large cohort studies, people who ate more eggs didn't die more often overall. Some analyses found a small higher risk, and one meta-analysis found more cancer deaths at the highest intakes. The evidence is low to moderate certainty.

findings.population: Adults without diabetes in cohort studies (meta-analyses of 16 cohorts, 589,559 people), in the US, Europe and Asia
whyThisGrade: Observational, with self-reported egg intake

The results split by region: a higher risk in US studies, consistent between them, and none in European or Asian studies. The authors think differences in how eggs are eaten, and with what, may explain it, but this hasn't been tested
Overall, results vary a lot between studies (heterogeneity 70%)
findings.summary: In three large US cohorts (213,798 people, 20,514 new cases of type 2 diabetes), each extra egg a day went with 14% higher risk (95% confidence interval 7% to 20%) after adjusting for updated BMI, lifestyle and diet. In the same paper's meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies (589,559 people), the pooled relative risk per egg a day was 1.07 (0.99 to 1.15) overall, but 1.18 (1.10 to 1.27) in US studies, 0.99 (0.85 to 1.15) in European ones and 0.82 (0.62 to 1.09) in Asian ones. An earlier meta-analysis with 39,610 Swedish men found the same split: per extra 3 eggs a week, 1.18 (1.13 to 1.24) in five US studies and 0.97 (0.90 to 1.05) in seven non-US studies, and no clear link in the Swedish men themselves. Both groups of authors suggest that egg-eating habits and the overall diet around eggs differ between populations.
findings.bottomLine: In US cohort studies, people who ate more eggs were more likely to develop type 2 diabetes; in European and Asian studies they weren't. Why isn't known: what eggs are eaten with may differ. These are links, not proof.

findings.population: Mostly healthy adults in randomised trials of eating more eggs against fewer or none (13 to 28 trials per analysis)
whyThisGrade: Many randomised trials, with consistent results and little variation between them in the 2020 meta-analysis (heterogeneity 18% for LDL)
Lowered: most trials were short (weeks to a few months), and the comparison diets differed

Some of the work on dietary cholesterol was funded by the egg industry: a 2019 meta-regression by the American Egg Board/Egg Nutrition Center, and a 2015 meta-analysis partly by the same funder. The 2020 egg meta-analysis was funded by a Taiwanese hospital and declared no conflicts
These are blood fats, not heart attacks: no trial has followed people long enough to count heart events
findings.summary: A 2018 meta-analysis of 28 trials found that eating eggs raised LDL cholesterol by 5.55 mg/dL (95% confidence interval 3.14 to 7.69), HDL cholesterol by 2.13 mg/dL (1.10 to 3.16) and total cholesterol by 5.60 mg/dL (3.11 to 8.09) compared with low-egg diets (5.55 mg/dL is about 0.14 mmol/L), with no change in the LDL-to-HDL ratio or triglycerides; part of the variation between trials was explained by people's response to dietary cholesterol. A 2020 meta-analysis of trials in healthy people found LDL 8.14 mg/dL (about 0.21 mmol/L) higher (4.46 to 11.82; 13 trials), no clear change in HDL (1.27, −0.28 to 2.83) and a slightly higher LDL-to-HDL ratio (0.14, 0.05 to 0.22), with larger effects in trials over 2 months. Across 55 trials of dietary cholesterol (2,652 people), each extra 100 mg a day was predicted to raise LDL by 1.90 to 4.58 mg/dL depending on the model. People differ: in trials adding 640 mg of cholesterol a day from eggs for 30 days, LDL and HDL didn't rise in 'hyporesponders' but both rose in 'hyperresponders' (40 men and 51 premenopausal women), while the LDL-to-HDL ratio stayed the same in the women and rose in the male hyperresponders. The American Heart Association's 2020 advisory concluded that most trial meta-analyses link cholesterol intakes above current average levels with higher total or LDL cholesterol.
findings.bottomLine: In trials, eating more eggs raised LDL cholesterol by about 5 to 8 mg/dL (about 0.14 to 0.21 mmol/L) on average, and HDL a little in some analyses. People differ: in some, blood cholesterol barely moves; in others ('hyperresponders') it rises more.

findings.outcome: Heart disease in people with type 2 diabetes
findings.population: Adults with type 2 diabetes in cohort studies, and adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in randomised trials of up to 12 months
whyThisGrade: Cohort results point to higher risk but are imprecise and vary a lot between studies (heterogeneity 65%); in the large US cohorts there was no clear link
Trials found no change in blood fats, blood sugar or inflammation, but they measured markers for up to 12 months, not heart attacks
The first DIABEGG trial phase was funded by the Australian Egg Corporation; the follow-up by Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council
findings.summary: A 2013 meta-analysis of cohort studies found that, in people with diabetes, eating at least one egg a day went with higher cardiovascular risk than eating less than one a week (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% confidence interval 1.09 to 2.62). The 2020 meta-analysis found a pooled relative risk of 1.25 (0.99 to 1.59) per extra egg a day and 1.40 (1.00 to 1.97) for high against low intake in people with type 2 diabetes, with considerable variation between studies; in its own three US cohorts, egg intake wasn't linked with heart disease in people with type 2 diabetes (1.06, 0.81 to 1.39 for at least one egg a day). In the DIABEGG trial, 140 people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes ate 2 eggs a day 6 days a week or fewer than 2 eggs a week for 3 months, with more unsaturated fats in both diets: HDL, LDL, total cholesterol, triglycerides and blood sugar control didn't differ. Over 12 months (128 people), glucose, HbA1c, blood fats and CRP still didn't differ. A 2017 review of 6 trials in people with or at risk of type 2 diabetes found that 6 to 12 eggs a week didn't change total or LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting glucose, insulin or CRP, and HDL rose in 4 of the 6.
findings.bottomLine: Some cohort studies found more heart disease in people with type 2 diabetes who ate more eggs, but results vary and are imprecise. Trials of up to 12 months found no change in their blood fats, blood sugar or CRP. Neither settles the question.

findings.outcome: Lutein in the blood and macular pigment in the eye
findings.population: Healthy adults and older adults in small trials (5 randomised trials, 296 people, in the pooled analysis)
whyThisGrade: Small, short trials (weeks to 4 months); one 90-day trial of 100 people found no change in macular pigment
Macular pigment is a measure in the eye, not a disease: no trial has tested whether eggs prevent age-related macular degeneration
Two of the trials (24 women; older adults taking statins) weren't described as randomised in their abstracts, and the statin study had no control group
Several trials used enriched eggs; one was funded by a company making an egg-yolk drink, and two of its authors held a patent on it
findings.summary: Lutein and zeaxanthin collect in the macula, the centre of the retina, where they may reduce damage from light; more of this macular pigment may lower the risk of age-related macular degeneration, but that hasn't been tested with eggs. A 2021 meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials (296 people) found that eating eggs raised macular pigment optical density (how much yellow pigment sits in the centre of the retina) by 0.037 (95% confidence interval 0.004 to 0.069) and serum lutein by 0.150 µmol/L (0.037 to 0.263), with no variation between trials. In 24 women eating 6 eggs a week for 12 weeks, serum zeaxanthin and macular pigment rose, while serum lutein and cholesterol didn't change. In older adults taking statins, 4 egg yolks a day for 5 weeks raised macular pigment by up to 50% in those who started low. In a 90-day trial of 100 people, lutein-enriched eggs raised serum lutein by 76% but macular pigment didn't change in any group. In the 4-month ALGOVUE trial (99 people), 2 eggs a day raised macular pigment slightly with standard or enriched eggs. In 10 men given 6 mg of lutein from different sources, more of it reached the blood from lutein-enriched eggs than from supplements or spinach.
findings.bottomLine: In small trials, eating eggs raised lutein in the blood and slightly increased the yellow pigment at the centre of the retina, which is thought to protect it. No trial has tested whether this prevents eye disease, and one trial found no change.

findings.outcome: TMAO, a gut-bacteria product of choline, in the blood
findings.population: Healthy adults and adults with metabolic syndrome in randomised trials (6 trials in the pooled analysis)
whyThisGrade: The 2025 meta-analysis authors rated the certainty moderate (NutriGRADE), lowered for imprecision and variation between trials; they declared no funding and no conflicts
Few, short trials; after single meals of 2 or more egg yolks, TMAO did rise in 6 volunteers
Whether TMAO itself causes heart disease is debated, so a change in TMAO wouldn't settle what eggs do to the heart
findings.summary: Eggs are one of the richest food sources of choline. TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) is made by gut bacteria and the liver from choline and has been linked with heart disease; whether it causes it is still debated. A 2025 meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials found no clear effect of eating eggs on fasting blood TMAO (−0.08 µmol/L, 95% confidence interval −0.47 to 0.32), choline or betaine, with moderate certainty. In a 4-week trial in 82 healthy young adults, 4 hard-boiled eggs a day didn't raise fasting TMAO or platelet reactivity, while choline bitartrate supplements with similar total choline raised both. After single breakfasts of 0 to 6 egg yolks in 6 volunteers, eating 2 or more raised TMAO in blood and urine in the following hours, with large differences between people, and no change in CRP or oxidised LDL.
findings.bottomLine: Eggs are rich in choline, which gut bacteria can turn into TMAO. In trials, eating eggs daily didn't clearly raise fasting TMAO, unlike choline supplements. Whether TMAO itself harms the heart is still debated.

whoShouldBeCareful.note: Egg allergy mostly starts in babies and young children. In a European birth cohort of 12,049 babies, about 1.2% had egg allergy confirmed by age 2 (from 0.07% in Greece to 2.18% in the UK), and half grew out of it within a year. In an Australian cohort, 471 of 5,276 one-year-olds had raw egg allergy, 89% of egg allergies had gone by age 6, and 1.2% of children still had it then. A meta-analysis of 5 trials (1,915 infants) found that egg introduced at 4 to 6 months went with less egg allergy (risk ratio 0.56; moderate certainty). Egg allergy, or a suspected one in a child, is something to discuss with a doctor or an allergy specialist.

Raw or partly cooked eggs can carry Salmonella, which in severe cases may cause miscarriage or premature labour. UK advice, summarised by the British Nutrition Foundation in 2025, is that eggs with the British Lion mark are very low risk and can be eaten raw or partly cooked in pregnancy, and that all other eggs be cooked until the white and yolk are solid. Outside the UK, the Lion mark doesn't apply, and local advice and safety schemes differ. A midwife or doctor can advise on food safety in pregnancy.

Some cohort studies found more heart disease in people with type 2 diabetes who ate more eggs (for example a hazard ratio of 1.69 for at least one egg a day in a 2013 meta-analysis), while others found no clear link, and trials of up to 12 months found no change in blood fats or blood sugar. With diabetes, how eggs fit into the whole diet is worth discussing with a doctor or dietitian.

cautions: Egg industry bodies funded several studies on this page: the DIABEGG trial's first phase (Australian Egg Corporation), the 2019 dietary cholesterol meta-regression (American Egg Board/Egg Nutrition Center), the 2015 dietary cholesterol meta-analysis in part (the same funder), and the review that gives the amounts of cholesterol and choline in an egg (British Egg Industry Council). Industry funding doesn't make a result wrong, but it is worth knowing.

In the US cohorts, people who ate more eggs also ate more bacon, other processed meat, red meat and refined grains. A link between eggs and disease in such studies may partly be a link with what eggs are eaten with.
Frying adds fat from the oil, and dishes made with eggs (cakes, quiches, mayonnaise) bring other ingredients; studies mostly counted eggs, not how they were cooked.
Lutein, choline and omega-3 enriched eggs differ from standard eggs in those compounds; the food table's numbers are for ordinary eggs.
Choline supplements and lutein capsules are not the same as eggs, and the findings on this page don't apply to them.
unknowns: Why cohort results differ between the US, Europe and Asia: differences in how many eggs people eat, how they're cooked and what they're eaten with are suspected, but not shown.
Whether the small rise in LDL cholesterol from eggs changes heart risk over decades: trials measured blood fats for weeks or months, and no trial has counted heart attacks or strokes.
Whether eggs are riskier for people with type 2 diabetes: cohort results point both ways and trials measured only blood markers, for up to 12 months.

Who is a 'hyperresponder' to dietary cholesterol: how much extra dietary cholesterol raises a person's blood cholesterol can't be accurately predicted in advance, and trials classified people only after measuring their response.
Whether lutein from eggs lowers the risk of age-related macular degeneration: trials measured pigment in the eye, not the disease.
Whether TMAO causes heart disease or only marks it: this is debated, so what TMAO changes would mean is unclear.
Why one meta-analysis found more cancer deaths with the highest egg intakes: this hasn't been explained, and it is a link from cohort studies.

Which of the egg's thousands of compounds matter: the food table tracks about 30, not cholesterol, choline, lutein or most others; the rest is nutritional dark matter, captured in studies of people eating eggs but not named.
